ECE 6390

Turbo coding and iterative decoding

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how interleaving and repeated soft decoding can recover structure missed by isolated decisions.

A parallel-concatenated turbo encoder supplies the systematic data and parity from two constituent encoders. The first sees the original input order; the second sees a known interleaved order. Transmitting one systematic bit and two parity bits per input gives nominal rate 1/3 before boundary overhead.

Interleaving rearranges positions without adding bits. It changes the context of troublesome local patterns. The receiver applies the matching permutation and inverse permutation when exchanging evidence. Puncturing omits specified coded positions to raise code rate; the receiver knows that omission pattern.

Turbo decoding uses soft-input/soft-output constituent decoders. Each combines channel evidence, code constraints and information from the other decoder, then passes the newly obtained contribution, called extrinsic information. Feeding the same evidence back as though it were new would overstate confidence. A loop of ordinary hard-output Viterbi decisions does not supply this probability exchange.

Iterations trade computation, energy and latency for better estimates; they do not guarantee correction of every error. A quoted performance curve needs the code, rate, channel, decoder, iteration limit and error-counting location. The lecture also discusses iterative demapping and decoding, where uncertain symbol labels can be revisited. The figure shows the architecture rather than simulating an unverified BER gain.

Example

If an unpunctured encoder transmits 300 coded bits for 100 information bits, its nominal rate is 1/3. Omitting 100 specified parity bits leaves 200 transmitted bits and rate 1/2, before termination or other framing costs. The surviving parity still constrains the same information sequence.

Practice

1. Which part of the turbo architecture adds redundancy: the interleaver or the parity encoders?

A permutation preserves the length of its input.

The parity encoders add the redundant constraints. The interleaver changes ordering and relationships but does not itself add bits.

2. Why exchange extrinsic evidence rather than repeatedly recycle the entire posterior as new evidence?

Track which observations were already used.

Reusing the same channel or prior evidence as though independent would double-count it and can create unjustified confidence. The exchanged contribution should represent the other decoder’s newly inferred information.
